papers.research_question: To what extent do multilingual pre-trained language models learn language-neutral representations, and what is the effect of such representations on cross-lingual transfer performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that multilingual language models contain language-neutral sub-networks that are topologically similar across languages and can be effectively transferred for cross-lingual tasks, but this transferability decreases at higher sparsity levels.
papers.conclusion: The results suggest that multilingual language models include separate language-neutral and language-specific components, with the language-neutral components playing a more prominent role in cross-lingual transfer performance.
papers.key_findings:
Winning tickets (sub-networks) can be found for each language and task at multiple sparsity levels, though performance degrades at higher sparsity.
Sub-networks for different languages have high parameter overlap, especially for NER and XNLI tasks, indicating language-neutral components.
Cross-lingual transfer of winning tickets is effective for XNLI and NER, but less so for MLM, and transfer performance degrades at higher sparsity.
The language-neutral components are more prominent in the middle to upper layers of the model.
Combining multiple languages during pruning can yield sub-networks that transfer better to low-resource languages.
papers.limitation:
Parameter overlap may not be a fine-grained measure for identifying language-neutral components, as small differences in cross-lingual performance do not strongly correlate with overlap.
Only the lottery ticket hypothesis is used for discovering sub-networks, while other pruning and masking methods may provide complementary or competing insights.
Due to computational limitations, the analysis is limited to three tasks and eleven languages, and new insights may emerge from a larger cross-section.
papers.abstract: Multilingual pre-trained language models transfer remarkably well on cross-lingual downstream tasks. However, the extent to which they learn language-neutral representations (i.e., shared representations that encode similar phenomena across languages), and the effect of such representations on cross-lingual transfer performance, remain open questions. In this work, we conceptualize language neutrality of multilingual models as a function of the overlap between language-encoding subnetworks of these models. We employ the lottery ticket hypothesis to discover sub-networks that are individually optimized for various languages and tasks. Our evaluation across three distinct tasks and eleven typologically-diverse languages demonstrates that sub-networks for different languages are topologically similar (i.e., language-neutral), making them effective initializations for cross-lingual transfer with limited performance degradation. 1

papers.title: Similarity of Sentence Representations in Multilingual LMs: Resolving Conflicting Literature and a Case Study of Baltic Languages
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models internally represent different languages, and do they converge to a shared cross-lingual space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper resolves conflicting literature by showing that multilingual LMs project languages into a shared cross-lingual space when using mean-pooling and CKA/SVCCA, and finds that Baltic languages are part of this space.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mean-pooling with SVCCA/CKA is optimal for cross-lingual representational similarity analysis, and while most languages share a cross-lingual space, Baltic languages are part of it.
papers.key_findings:
CLS-pooling with PWCCA gives divergent patterns, while mean-pooling with CKA/SVCCA shows convergence in cross-lingual similarity.
Mean-pooling is more effective than CLS-pooling for cross-lingual representational analysis, as shown by probing tasks.
Not all languages share the cross-lingual space equally; some like Urdu and Hindi are outliers.
Baltic languages (Estonian, Latvian, Lithuanian) are grouped and belong to the shared cross-lingual space.
The most cross-lingual layer for XLM-R is the 7th layer.
future_direction: Finding the exact criteria for exclusion of languages from the shared cross-lingual space.
papers.abstract: Low-resource languages, such as Baltic languages, benefit from Large Multilingual Models (LMs) that possess remarkable cross-lingual transfer performance capabilities. This work is an interpretation and analysis study into cross-lingual representations of Multilingual LMs. Previous works hypothesized that these LMs internally project representations of different languages into a shared cross-lingual space. However, the literature produced contradictory results. In this paper, we revisit the prior work claiming that "BERT is not an Interlingua" and show that different languages do converge to a shared space in such language models with another choice of pooling strategy or similarity index. Then, we perform cross-lingual representational analysis for the two most popular multilingual LMs employing 378 pairwise language comparisons. We discover that while most languages share joint cross-lingual space, some do not. However, we observe that Baltic languages do belong to that shared space.

papers.title: Exploring Multilingual Probing in Large Language Models: A Cross-Language Analysis
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether other languages achieve comparable probing accuracy to English, whether they exhibit similar layer-wise behavioral patterns to English, and what the similarities are between probing vectors across different languages.
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends probing techniques to a multilingual context and reveals significant disparities in LLMs' performance and representational qualities between high-resource and low-resource languages.
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight significant disparities in LLMs' multilingual capabilities and suggest that these models may not be learning deeper linguistic concepts effectively across all languages, especially low-resource ones.
papers.key_findings:
High-resource languages achieve higher probing accuracy than low-resource languages.
High-resource languages exhibit similar layer-wise trends to English, with accuracy improving in deeper layers, while low-resource languages show stable or only slight improvement.
Probing vectors of high-resource languages are more similar to each other, while low-resource languages have lower similarities among themselves and with high-resource languages.
papers.limitation:
Using machine translation to generate prompts and questions may introduce noise.
Only five open-source LLMs and two datasets are experimented with, limiting generalizability.
Only linear classifier probing is used; more sophisticated probing methods could offer deeper insights.
future_direction: Develop more equitable and effective multilingual language models that can better capture universal linguistic concepts.
Extend the research to multimodal models that incorporate visual and textual information.
Explore more sophisticated probing methods beyond linear classifiers.
papers.abstract: Probing techniques for large language models (LLMs) have primarily focused on English, overlooking the vast majority of the world's languages. In this paper, we extend these probing methods to a multilingual context, investigating the behaviors of LLMs across diverse languages. We conduct experiments on several open-source LLM models, analyzing probing accuracy, trends across layers, and similarities between probing vectors for multiple languages. Our key findings reveal: (1) a consistent performance gap between high-resource and low-resource languages, with high-resource languages achieving significantly higher probing accuracy; (2) divergent layer-wise accuracy trends, where high-resource languages show substantial improvement in deeper layers similar to English; and (3) higher representational similarities among high-resource languages, with low-resource languages demonstrating lower similarities both among themselves and with high-resource languages. These results highlight significant disparities in LLMs' multilingual capabilities and emphasize the need for improved modeling of low-resource languages.

papers.title: I Spy With My Model's Eye: Visual Search as a Behavioural Test for MLLMs
papers.research_question: Does the visual processing of multimodal large language models exhibit human-like pop-out effects and capacity limits in visual search tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces visual search paradigms as a cognitively grounded diagnostic tool for evaluating perceptual capabilities in MLLMs, finding that advanced models exhibit human-like pop-out effects and capacity limits in conjunctive search.
papers.conclusion: Visual search tasks provide a valuable behavioural test for understanding MLLM perceptual capabilities and can serve as a cognitively grounded diagnostic tool.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-4o exhibits human-like pop-out effects in disjunctive search tasks (e.g., large target among smaller ones) with set-size independent accuracy.
MLLMs show capacity limits in conjunctive search tasks, with accuracy declining as distractor set size increases.
Some MLLMs incorporate natural scene priors, such as a bias for vertical lighting gradients and better detection of bottom-lit spheres.
Fine-tuning on conjunctive search tasks improves performance and generalizes to out-of-distribution set sizes and similar shape tasks.
Mechanistic interpretability reveals that disjunctive search tasks are resolved in earlier layers, while conjunctive tasks require deeper layers.
papers.limitation: Fine-tuning on conjunctive search tasks improves performance but does not reach pop-out levels.
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance on vision-language tasks, yet their visual processing is opaque. Most black-box evaluations measure task accuracy, but reveal little about underlying mechanisms. Drawing on cognitive psychology, we adapt classic visual search paradigms -- originally developed to study human perception -- to test whether MLLMs exhibit the ``pop-out'' effect, where salient visual features are detected independently of distractor set size. Using controlled experiments targeting colour, size and lighting features, we find that advanced MLLMs exhibit human-like pop-out effects in colour or size-based disjunctive (single feature) search, as well as capacity limits for conjunctive (multiple feature) search. We also find evidence to suggest that MLLMs, like humans, incorporate natural scene priors such as lighting direction into object representations. We reinforce our findings using targeted fine-tuning and mechanistic interpretability analyses. Our work shows how visual search can serve as a cognitively grounded diagnostic tool for evaluating perceptual capabilities in MLLMs.

papers.title: Understanding the role of FFNs in driving multilingual behaviour in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) in large language models drive multilingual behavior, and what are the patterns of multilingual processing across layers and model sizes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the metric 'activation flatness' and analyzes FFN sublayers (detectors and combinators) to reveal distinct patterns of multilingual processing, identifying the phenomenon of 'over-layerization' where increasing layer depth without other adjustments can degrade performance.
papers.conclusion: The analysis reveals distinct patterns in FFN sublayers for multilingual processing, with detectors becoming more peaked and language-specific in later layers, and combinators showing multilingual behavior in middle layers, while also identifying over-layerization in certain model configurations.
papers.key_findings:
FFN representations are more sparse near the input and output layers across all models.
Detector activations become more peaked (less flat) through the layers, while combinator activations show a distinct drop in flatness around layer 20 regardless of model size.
Early detector layers are multilingual and process shallow features, becoming more language-specific near the output.
Combinator layers are mostly multilingual in the middle layers, with the final layers becoming language-specific, especially in larger models.
The 2.9B parameter model exhibits 'over-layerization', where increased layer depth without corresponding adjustments leads to degraded generation quality compared to the 7.5B model.
papers.limitation:
The analysis relies only on model snapshots (activations), which does not fully capture the complexities of LLMs; probing tasks or attention matrices could provide a more comprehensive understanding.
The investigation is limited to the XGLM model family, and findings may not generalize to other LLM architectures or implementations.
The analysis is limited to a set of predefined languages and test sets, which may not fully represent linguistic diversity.
future_direction: Investigate whether flatter activation patterns are easier to adapt in QLoRA fine-tuning.
Extend the analysis to more languages and explore cross-linguistic variation in more detail.
papers.abstract: Multilingualism in Large Language Models (LLMs) is an yet under-explored area. In this paper, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the multilingual capabilities of a family of a Large Language Model, examining its architecture, activation patterns, and processing mechanisms across languages. We introduce novel metrics to probe the model's multilingual behaviour at different layers and shed light on the impact of architectural choices on multilingual processing. Our findings reveal different patterns of multilinugal processing in the sublayers of Feed-Forward Networks of the models. Furthermore, we uncover the phenomenon of "over-layerization" in certain model configurations, where increasing layer depth without corresponding adjustments to other parameters may degrade model performance. Through comparisons within and across languages, we demonstrate the interplay between model architecture, layer depth, and multilingual processing capabilities of LLMs trained on multiple languages.

papers.title: Causal Analysis of Syntactic Agreement Neurons in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: How and where do multilingual language models encode syntactic agreement? Are neurons shared across languages and structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper extends causal probing to multilingual language models, finding two distinct layer-wise effect patterns for syntactic agreement depending on distance, significant neuron overlap across languages in autoregressive multilingual models but not masked language models, and that behavioral analyses underestimate masked language models' sensitivity to syntax.
papers.conclusion: Causal probing reveals distinct mechanisms for short- and long-range syntactic agreement in multilingual models, with autoregressive models showing more cross-lingual neuron sharing than masked models, and suggests that models encode syntax similarly across languages but with language-specific neurons.
papers.key_findings:
Two distinct layer-wise effect patterns for syntactic agreement: one for short-range (adjacent subject-verb) and one for long-range (separated by other tokens).
Neurons are shared across syntactic structures but not with semantic baselines, indicating abstract syntactic agreement encoding.
In autoregressive language models (XGLM), there is significant neuron overlap across languages, but in masked language models (mBERT), neurons are rarely shared across languages.
Neuron sparsity differs across structures (more sparse for short-range agreement) but not across languages.
Behavioral analyses likely underestimate how sensitive masked language models are to syntactic information because negative interference from other neurons masks strong syntax-sensitive neurons.
papers.limitation:
Limited to stimuli where subjects and verbs are single tokens, restricting the range of words and languages that can be studied.
Probing individual neurons may oversimplify because complex phenomena like syntactic agreement are likely encoded in sets of neurons.
future_direction: Developing methods for multi-token interventions and variable-length sequences.
Probing multiple neurons simultaneously to causally implicate model regions rather than individual components.
Investigating redundantly encoded syntactic information across neurons.
papers.abstract: Structural probing work has found evidence for latent syntactic information in pre-trained language models. However, much of this analysis has focused on monolingual models, and analyses of multilingual models have employed correlational methods that are confounded by the choice of probing tasks. In this study, we causally probe multilingual language models (XGLM and multilingual BERT) as well as monolingual BERT-based models across various languages; we do this by performing counterfactual perturbations on neuron activations and observing the effect on models' subject-verb agreement probabilities. We observe where in the model and to what extent syntactic agreement is encoded in each language. We find significant neuron overlap across languages in autoregressive multilingual language models, but not masked language models. We also find two distinct layer-wise effect patterns and two distinct sets of neurons used for syntactic agreement, depending on whether the subject and verb are separated by other tokens. Finally, we find that behavioral analyses of language models are likely underestimating how sensitive masked language models are to syntactic information.

papers.title: Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English?
papers.research_question: Do multilingual LLMs perform key reasoning steps in a representation space closest to English, regardless of input and output languages?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual LLMs perform semantic reasoning in a representation space biased towards English, even for non-English inputs and outputs, as evidenced by logit lens analysis and more effective steering with English-derived vectors.
papers.conclusion: Semantic decisions in LLMs are predominantly made in a representation space close to English, while non-lexical words are processed in the prompt language, and this behavior varies across models.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs route lexical words through English representation space before translating to the target language, while non-lexical words are not necessarily routed through English.
Steering non-English prompts is more effective using English steering vectors than vectors derived from the target language.
Facts are encoded in similar layers across languages, but models have a propensity to answer in English.
The degree of English-routing varies with model multilingualism and size, with more multilingual models routing less through English.
The latent representation structure allows interpolation between facts expressed in different languages while maintaining correctness, indicating shared semantic representations with language-specific components.
papers.limitation:
Tokenization varies across languages, complicating cross-lingual comparisons.
Models may have language confidence and confusion, affecting analysis.
Interpretability methods like steering depend on prompt steerability and may push activations outside the expected distribution.
Alternative methods like sparse autoencoders were not explored due to computational constraints.
future_direction: Developing more robust evaluation procedures for interpretability methods.
Exploring alternative methods like sparse autoencoders for cross-lingual analysis.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have multilingual capabilities and can solve tasks across various languages. However, we show that current LLMs make key decisions in a representation space closest to English, regardless of their input and output languages. Exploring the internal representations with a logit lens for sentences in French, German, Dutch, and Mandarin, we show that the LLM first emits representations close to English for semantically-loaded words before translating them into the target language. We further show that activation steering in these LLMs is more effective when the steering vectors are computed in English rather than in the language of the inputs and outputs. This suggests that multilingual LLMs perform key reasoning steps in a representation that is heavily shaped by English in a way that is not transparent to system users.

papers.title: What Language(s) Does Aya-23 Think In? How Multilinguality Affects Internal Language Representations
papers.research_question: How does balanced multilingual training affect internal language processing in LLMs, specifically in terms of language activation, neuron sharing, and layer-wise distribution of language-specific neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Balanced multilingual training leads to distinct internal language processing, with language-specific neurons concentrated in final layers and activation of typologically related languages during translation, unlike English-centric models.
papers.conclusion: Balanced multilingual training fundamentally alters how decoder-only LLMs process language internally, leading to language-specific neurons concentrated in final layers and activation of multiple languages during translation.
papers.key_findings:
Aya-23 activates typologically related language representations during translation, unlike English-centric models that rely on a single pivot language.
Code-mixed neuron activation patterns vary with mixing rates and are shaped more by the base language than the mixed-in one.
Aya-23’s language-specific neurons for code-mixed inputs concentrate in final layers, diverging from prior findings on decoder-only models.
Neuron overlap analysis shows that script similarity and typological relations impact processing across model types.
French-based code-mixed inputs show higher neuron clustering than Chinese-based inputs across all models, regardless of training data composition.
papers.limitation:
Token overlap between languages in the logit lens experiments may affect analysis of language-specific activation patterns.
Neuron specialization analysis using binary activations results in information loss that may obscure subtle activation patterns.
Code-mixed dataset created via rule-based word-to-word translation produces unnatural sentences that may not represent authentic code-switching.
Analysis is limited to three models and may not generalize to other architectures or sizes.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at multilingual tasks, yet their internal language processing remains poorly understood. We analyze how Aya-23-8B, a decoder-only LLM trained on balanced multilingual data, handles code-mixed, cloze, and translation tasks compared to predominantly monolingual models like Llama 3 and Chinese-LLaMA-2. Using logit lens and neuron specialization analyses, we find: (1) Aya-23 activates typologically related language representations during translation, unlike English-centric models that rely on a single pivot language; (2) code-mixed neuron activation patterns vary with mixing rates and are shaped more by the base language than the mixed-in one; and (3) Aya-23's languagespecific neurons for code-mixed inputs concentrate in final layers, diverging from prior findings on decoder-only models. Neuron overlap analysis further shows that script similarity and typological relations impact processing across model types. These findings reveal how multilingual training shapes LLM internals and inform future cross-lingual transfer research.

papers.title: Probing Multimodal Large Language Models for Global and Local Semantic Representations
papers.research_question: How is global and local semantic information encoded in decoder-only Multimodal Large Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: Intermediate layers of decoder-only MLLMs encode more global semantic information, while top layers focus excessively on local token features, diminishing global encoding ability.
papers.conclusion: The upper layers in MLLMs focus too much on the next token's semantic features, resulting in loss of global information, which should inform future pre-training improvements.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers of MLLMs perform best on global image-text entailment tasks.
Top layers may excessively focus on local information, leading to diminished ability to encode global information.
In object recognition, upper layers show improved performance when provided with category cues, indicating a focus on local features.
The findings are consistent across different MLLMs and various prompts, indicating robustness.
future_direction: Improving pre-training processes and architecture designs of MLLMs to better encode global information.
papers.abstract: The advancement of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has greatly accelerated the development of applications in understanding integrated texts and images. Recent works leverage image-caption datasets to train MLLMs, achieving state-of-the-art performance on image-to-text tasks. However, there are few studies exploring which layers of MLLMs make the most effort to the global image information, which plays vital roles in multimodal comprehension and generation. In this study, we find that the intermediate layers of models can encode more global semantic information, whose representation vectors perform better on visual-language entailment tasks, rather than the topmost layers. We further probe models regarding local semantic representations through object recognition tasks. We find that the topmost layers may excessively focus on local information, leading to a diminished ability to encode global information. Our code and data are released via https://github.com/kobayashikanna01/probing_MLLM_rep.

papers.title: Cross-modal Associations in Vision and Language Models: Revisiting the Bouba-Kiki Effect
papers.research_question: Do vision-and-language models (VLMs) exhibit human-like cross-modal associations, specifically the bouba-kiki effect?
papers.core_contribution: CLIP models (ResNet and ViT) do not show consistent human-like cross-modal associations (bouba-kiki effect), and their internal representations lack the robust modality integration seen in humans.
papers.conclusion: VLMs do not exhibit human-like cross-modal associations, highlighting limitations in their internal representations and alignment with human intuitions.
papers.key_findings:
Neither CLIP ResNet nor ViT consistently exhibit the bouba-kiki effect across different prompts and pseudoword sets.
Models can correctly associate English adjectives with corresponding shapes (baseline), but fail for pseudowords.
Grad-CAM analysis shows that models do not attend to shape-specific features when processing pseudowords.
Models' predictions are inconsistent and often collapse to a few labels, indicating lack of robust cross-modal associations.
The models' performance is at chance level for the bouba-kiki task, in contrast to humans who show strong preferences.
papers.limitation:
Only tested on CLIP versions, not on more capable proprietary models.
Relies on text (orthographic) presentation of pseudowords, which may not capture auditory aspects of the bouba-kiki effect.
future_direction: Exploring cross-modal associations in more contemporary models (e.g., those with alignment layers).
Investigating audio-visual models to understand how different modalities contribute.
Incorporating cross-linguistic studies to account for cultural variation.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal models have raised questions about whether vision-and-language models (VLMs) integrate cross-modal information in ways that reflect human cognition. One well-studied test case in this domain is the bouba-kiki effect, where humans reliably associate pseudowords like `bouba' with round shapes and `kiki' with jagged ones. Given the mixed evidence found in prior studies for this effect in VLMs, we present a comprehensive re-evaluation focused on two variants of CLIP, ResNet and Vision Transformer (ViT), given their centrality in many state-of-the-art VLMs. We apply two complementary methods closely modelled after human experiments: a prompt-based evaluation that uses probabilities as a measure of model preference, and we use Grad-CAM as a novel approach to interpret visual attention in shape-word matching tasks. Our findings show that these model variants do not consistently exhibit the bouba-kiki effect. While ResNet shows a preference for round shapes, overall performance across both model variants lacks the expected associations. Moreover, direct comparison with prior human data on the same task shows that the models' responses fall markedly short of the robust, modality-integrated behaviour characteristic of human cognition. These results contribute to the ongoing debate about the extent to which VLMs truly understand cross-modal concepts, highlighting limitations in their internal representations and alignment with human intuitions.

papers.title: Tracing the Roots of Facts in Multilingual Language Models: Independent, Shared, and Transferred Knowledge
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how multilingual language models acquire and represent factual knowledge across languages, specifically examining the factors affecting probing performance, whether fact representations are shared or independent across languages, and how cross-lingual representations are formed.
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes methods for distinguishing three types of fact representations in multilingual language models (language-independent, cross-lingual shared, and cross-lingual transferred) and reveals the challenges in cross-lingual factual knowledge transfer.
papers.conclusion: Our research establishes the groundwork for further studies in understanding cross-lingual factual knowledge representation and highlights the challenges in achieving effective cross-lingual transfer of factual knowledge from high-resource to low-resource languages in ML-LMs.
papers.key_findings:
Factual probing performance across languages shows moderate correlation with training data volume and strong negative correlation with mask token count.
There are localized knowledge sharing patterns among geographically proximate languages.
ML-LMs exhibit both language-independent and cross-lingual fact representations, even for the same fact.
Active fact neurons in low-resource languages are more active and distributed in shallow layers compared to high-resource languages.
Cross-lingual transfer of factual knowledge does occur but is limited, and many correctly predicted facts in low-resource languages can be attributed to simple inference patterns rather than true transfer.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to encoder-based models (mBERT and XLM-R) and may not generalize to large decoder-based multilingual models.
future_direction: Enhance the cross-lingual fact representation learning in ML-LMs.
Develop a more precise factual probing dataset.
papers.abstract: Acquiring factual knowledge for language models (LMs) in low-resource languages poses a serious challenge, thus resorting to cross-lingual transfer in multilingual LMs (ML-LMs).In this study, we ask how ML-LMs acquire and represent factual knowledge.Using the multilingual factual knowledge probing dataset, mLAMA, we first conducted a neuron investigation of ML-LMs (specifically, multilingual BERT).We then traced the roots of facts back to the knowledge source (Wikipedia) to identify the ways in which ML-LMs acquire specific facts.We finally identified three patterns of acquiring and representing facts in ML-LMs: languageindependent, cross-lingual shared and transferred, and devised methods for differentiating them.Our findings highlight the challenge of maintaining consistent factual knowledge across languages, underscoring the need for better fact representation learning in ML-LMs. 1

papers.title: When Alignment Hurts: Decoupling Representational Spaces in Multilingual Models
papers.research_question: Does alignment with a high-resource standard language always benefit related low-resource varieties? The paper challenges this assumption by showing that excessive representational entanglement can hinder generative modeling.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an online variational probing framework for subspace decoupling, providing causal evidence that representational entanglement with a high-resource language hinders generative modeling for low-resource varieties.
papers.conclusion: This work demonstrates that representational entanglement with a high-resource language is a critical and addressable bottleneck for generative modeling in closely-related, low-resource language varieties, and provides a causal intervention method to mitigate it.
papers.key_findings:
Excessive representational entanglement with Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) hinders generative performance for low-resource Arabic dialects.
Better generative performance correlates with greater representational separability from MSA in the model's internal geometry.
The proposed online subspace decoupling intervention improves dialectal generation by up to +4.9 chrF++ on individual dialects and +2.0 on average compared to standard fine-tuning.
The intervention leads to a trade-off, with a measured decrease in standard-language (MSA) generation performance.
The method is effective across 25 Arabic dialects, demonstrating the generalizability of the representational dominance phenomenon.
papers.limitation:
The MADAR dataset is composed of relatively short sentences, which may not fully capture model behaviors on tasks requiring longer-form generation.
The causal claim is based on intervention experiments within a single language family (Arabic), and generalization to other language families requires further validation.
future_direction: Scalable and Efficient Methods
Inference-Time Interventions
Generalization to Other Languages
papers.abstract: Alignment with high-resource standard languages is often assumed to aid the modeling of related low-resource varieties. We challenge this assumption by demonstrating that excessive representational entanglement with a dominant variety, such as Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) in relation to Arabic dialects, can actively hinder generative modeling. We present the first comprehensive causal study of this phenomenon by analyzing and directly intervening in the internal representation geometry of large language models (LLMs). Our key contribution is an online variational probing framework that continuously estimates the subspace of the standard variety during fine-tuning, enabling projection-based decoupling from this space. While our study uses Arabic as a case due to its unusually rich parallel resources across 25 dialects, the broader motivation is methodological: dialectal MT serves as a controlled proxy for generative tasks where comparable multi-variety corpora are unavailable. Across 25 dialects, our intervention improves generation quality by up to +4.9 chrF++ and +2.0 on average compared to standard fine-tuning, despite a measured tradeoff in standard-language performance. These results provide causal evidence that subspace dominance by high-resource varieties can restrict generative capacity for related varieties. More generally, we unify geometric and information-theoretic probing with subspace-level causal interventions, offering practical tools for improving generative modeling in closely related language families and, more broadly, for controlling representational allocation in multilingual and multi-domain LLMs. Code will be released.

papers.title: Under the Shadow of Babel: How Language Shapes Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Do different languages lead LLMs to think differently? Do LLMs internalize the cognitive biases embedded in different languages, specifically in causal reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces BICAUSE, a structured bilingual dataset for causal reasoning, and provides empirical evidence that LLMs internalize language-specific reasoning biases, showing typologically aligned attention patterns and a shared understanding when reasoning succeeds.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit language-specific biases in causal reasoning that impact performance, but when reasoning succeeds, they form a shared understanding that transcends surface linguistic form.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit typologically aligned attention patterns, focusing more on causes and sentence-initial connectives in Chinese, while showing a more balanced distribution in English.
Models internalize language-specific preferences for causal word order and often rigidly apply them to atypical inputs, leading to degraded performance, especially in Chinese.
When causal reasoning succeeds, model representations converge toward semantically aligned abstractions across languages, indicating a shared understanding beyond surface form.
Attention patterns over syntactic components show consistent layerwise trends but differ in absolute weights between Chinese and English, reflecting language-specific structural biases.
The similarity of layerwise attention patterns (measured by SVCCA) correlates with reasoning accuracy across different input structures and languages.
papers.limitation:
Focuses exclusively on Chinese and English, representing only a small portion of the world's linguistic diversity.
Does not encompass all model architectures or training paradigms.
Primarily focuses on attention patterns and hidden representations; does not incorporate additional interpretability methods.
future_direction: Extending BICAUSE to a broader set of languages.
Advancing research on multilingual interpretability and alignment mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Language is not only a tool for communication but also a medium for human cognition and reasoning. If, as linguistic relativity suggests, the structure of language shapes cognitive patterns, then large language models (LLMs) trained on human language may also internalize the habitual logical structures embedded in different languages. To examine this hypothesis, we introduce BICAUSE, a structured bilingual dataset for causal reasoning, which includes semantically aligned Chinese and English samples in both forward and reversed causal forms. Our study reveals three key findings: (1) LLMs exhibit typologically aligned attention patterns, focusing more on causes and sentence-initial connectives in Chinese, while showing a more balanced distribution in English. (2) Models internalize language-specific preferences for causal word order and often rigidly apply them to atypical inputs, leading to degraded performance, especially in Chinese. (3) When causal reasoning succeeds, model representations converge toward semantically aligned abstractions across languages, indicating a shared understanding beyond surface form. Overall, these results suggest that LLMs not only mimic surface linguistic forms but also internalize the reasoning biases shaped by language. Rooted in cognitive linguistic theory, this phenomenon is for the first time empirically verified through structural analysis of model internals.

papers.title: When Meanings Meet: Investigating the Emergence and Quality of Shared Concept Spaces during Multilingual Language Model Training
papers.research_question: How do shared, language-agnostic concept spaces emerge and develop during the multilingual pretraining of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Shared concept spaces emerge early in multilingual pretraining and remain relatively stable, but alignment with these spaces is language-dependent and influenced by training data composition.
papers.conclusion: Shared concept spaces emerge early and are progressively refined during multilingual pretraining, with alignment depending on language and data composition. Targeted multi-aligned data can improve alignment for low-resource languages.
papers.key_findings:
Shared concept spaces arise early in pretraining and continue to refine throughout training.
Alignment with shared concept spaces depends on language similarity and training data proportion.
Cross-lingual concept patching can shift model behavior, such as selecting dominant senses for polysemous words or translating cross-lingual homographs instead of copying them.
The model initially prefers copying input words over translating them, a behavior learned early.
Patching from averaged representations across languages (the 'seen' setting) is often as effective as patching from English-only representations for inducing concepts in English output.
papers.limitation:
Focuses primarily on a single, relatively small model (EuroLLM-1.7B), though provides supporting evidence on two others.
Analysis is restricted to nouns; behavior of other word classes is not studied.
Inherits biases from the Multi-SimLex dataset, such as ambiguous translations for polysemous words.
Focuses only on the simple task of word-level translation; findings may not generalize to more complex tasks.
future_direction: Investigate how representations for other word classes (beyond nouns) behave.
Study the emergence and behavior of language-agnostic spaces for more complex multilingual tasks like sentence-level translation or reasoning.
papers.abstract: Training Large Language Models (LLMs) with high multilingual coverage is becoming increasingly important -- especially when monolingual resources are scarce. Recent studies have found that LLMs process multilingual inputs in shared concept spaces, thought to support generalization and cross-lingual transfer. However, these prior studies often do not use causal methods, lack deeper error analysis or focus on the final model only, leaving open how these spaces emerge during training. We investigate the development of language-agnostic concept spaces during pretraining of EuroLLM through the causal interpretability method of activation patching. We isolate cross-lingual concept representations, then inject them into a translation prompt to investigate how consistently translations can be altered, independently of the language. We find that shared concept spaces emerge early} and continue to refine, but that alignment with them is language-dependent}. Furthermore, in contrast to prior work, our fine-grained manual analysis reveals that some apparent gains in translation quality reflect shifts in behavior -- like selecting senses for polysemous words or translating instead of copying cross-lingual homographs -- rather than improved translation ability. Our findings offer new insight into the training dynamics of cross-lingual alignment and the conditions under which causal interpretability methods offer meaningful insights in multilingual contexts.

papers.title: Probing Contextual Language Models for Common Ground with Visual\n Representations
papers.research_question: To what extent are contextual representations of concrete nouns aligned with corresponding visual representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a probing method to measure the alignment between contextual language representations and visual features, finding that language representations provide a strong signal for retrieving image patches and that context plays an important role.
papers.conclusion: Contextual language models are useful for discerning between visual representations, but there is a large gap between model and human performance, indicating room for improvement in grounding language models.
papers.key_findings:
Contextual language models (e.g., BERT) significantly outperform non-contextual embeddings (e.g., GloVe) in instance-level retrieval of image patches.
Language representations alone can retrieve image patches of the correct object category with high recall (84-90%).
Contextual information, especially adjectives, improves instance retrieval accuracy.
Visually grounded language models (e.g., VILBERT-MT) slightly outperform text-only models in instance retrieval.
All examined models lag significantly behind human performance in instance retrieval.
papers.limitation: The examined models significantly underperform human subjects in instance retrieval.
papers.abstract:
The success of large-scale contextual language models has attracted great
interest in probing what is encoded in their representations. In this work, we
consider a new question: to what extent contextual representations of concrete
nouns are aligned with corresponding visual representations? We design a
probing model that evaluates how effective are text-only representations in
distinguishing between matching and non-matching visual representations. Our
findings show that language representations alone provide a strong signal for
retrieving image patches from the correct object categories. Moreover, they are
effective in retrieving specific instances of image patches; textual context
plays an important role in this process. Visually grounded language models
slightly outperform text-only language models in instance retrieval, but
greatly under-perform humans. We hope our analyses inspire future research in
understanding and improving the visual capabilities of language models.

papers.title: Tracing Multilingual Representations in LLMs with Cross-Layer Transcoders
papers.research_question: Do multilingual LLMs form shared representations across languages with language-specific decoding, and why does performance favor the dominant training language such as English?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual LLMs form a shared language-agnostic representation space in middle layers, with language-specific decoding in late layers; performance gaps are mechanistically explained by tokenizer bias and feature strength differences.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual LLMs use shared representations in middle layers and language-specific decoding in late layers, with performance gaps explained by feature strength and tokenizer bias.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual LLMs consistently form a shared language-agnostic space in middle layers, regardless of English dominance in training data.
Language-specific decoding depends on a small set of high-frequency features in late layers that linearly encode language identity from early layers.
Non-English performance failures are linked to dim late-layer features, weak middle-layer clusters, and tokenizer bias forcing early layers to specialize in word reassembly.
Finetuning strengthens these features and their connections, improving token assembly and language-specific decoding.
The shared multilingual space emerges as an architectural property, even when models are trained without English.
papers.abstract: Multilingual Large Language Models (LLMs) can process many languages, yet how they internally represent this diversity remains unclear. Do they form shared multilingual representations with language-specific decoding, and if so, why does performance favor the dominant training language? To address this, we train models on different multilingual mixtures and analyze their internal mechanisms using Cross-Layer Transcoders (CLTs) and Attribution Graphs. Our results reveal multilingual shared representations: the model employs highly similar features across languages, while language-specific decoding emerges in later layers. Training models without English shows identical multilingual shared space structures. Decoding relies partly on a small set of high-frequency features in the final layers, which linearly encode language identity from early layers. Intervening on these features allows one language to be suppressed and another substituted. Finally, to explain non-English failures, we perform a Model-Diffing experiment: underperformance arises from dim late-layer features, weak middle-layer clusters, and tokenizer bias toward English that forces early layers to specialize in word reassembly. Finetuning strengthens these features and their links, improving token assembly and language-specific decoding, providing a mechanistic explanation for multilingual gaps. Our models and CLTs are available at https://huggingface.co/collections/CausalNLP/multilingual-clts and https://huggingface.co/collections/CausalNLP/multilingual-gpt2-models. Our code is available at: https://github.com/abirharrasse/MultilingualCLTs

papers.title: What does it mean to be language-agnostic? Probing multilingual sentence encoders for typological properties
papers.research_question: How do multilingual sentence encoders capture typological properties of languages, and how does this vary with different pretraining strategies?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual sentence encoders capture typological properties, but the encoding differs based on pretraining objectives: models with cross-lingual objectives (LASER, XLM) lose typological information in higher layers and create a shared interlingual space, while models with monolingual objectives (M-BERT, XLM-R) retain typological information in all layers and partition the space into language-specific subspaces.
papers.conclusion: There is a trade-off between universality and language-specific information in multilingual encoders, and pretraining objectives influence how typological information is encoded.
papers.key_findings:
All encoders capture some typological properties (word order, pronouns, negation).
M-BERT and XLM-R outperform LASER and XLM on lexical and morphological properties.
Typological information is localizable in lower layers of LASER and XLM, but spread across all layers in M-BERT and XLM-R.
Cross-lingual training leads to more language-agnostic representations but at the cost of losing language-specific typological information in higher layers.
XLM generalizes to languages unseen during pretraining, capturing their typological properties.
papers.abstract: Multilingual sentence encoders have seen much success in cross-lingual model transfer for downstream NLP tasks. Yet, we know relatively little about the properties of individual languages or the general patterns of linguistic variation that they encode. We propose methods for probing sentence representations from state-of-the-art multilingual encoders (LASER, M-BERT, XLM and XLM-R) with respect to a range of typological properties pertaining to lexical, morphological and syntactic structure. In addition, we investigate how this information is distributed across all layers of the models. Our results show interesting differences in encoding linguistic variation associated with different pretraining strategies.

papers.title: The Geometry of Categorical and Hierarchical Concepts in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can the linear representation hypothesis be extended to represent categorical and hierarchical concepts in large language models, and how are hierarchical relationships encoded geometrically in the representation space?
papers.core_contribution: Extends the linear representation hypothesis to represent binary features as vectors and categorical concepts as polytopes, and proves that hierarchical relationships between concepts are encoded as orthogonality in the representation space.
papers.conclusion: The representation space of large language models encodes hierarchical semantic structure through a simple direct sum of polytopes, where hierarchical relations correspond to orthogonality.
papers.key_findings:
Binary features can be represented as vectors in the transformed representation space, with words belonging to the feature having similar projections onto the vector.
Categorical concepts are represented as polytopes, where vertices correspond to vector representations of the concept's elements.
Hierarchical relationships (e.g., parent-child) are geometrically encoded as orthogonality between the corresponding vector representations.
Empirical validation on Gemma and LLaMA-3 models shows the estimated vector representations for WordNet concepts align with the semantic hierarchy, exhibiting the predicted orthogonal structure.
The canonical representation space (using a causal inner product) is necessary to observe the hierarchical orthogonality; it does not hold under the naive Euclidean inner product.
papers.limitation:
The analysis and whitening transformation are limited to the final layer representation; understanding the geometry of internal layers remains an open question.
Perfect linear representations as defined may not be found by gradient descent in practice; the theory assumes their existence.
future_direction: Extending the geometric analysis to the internal layers of language models.
Designing interpretability methods (e.g., sparse autoencoders) that explicitly account for the hierarchical structure of semantic concepts.
papers.abstract: The linear representation hypothesis is the informal idea that semantic concepts are encoded as linear directions in the representation spaces of large language models (LLMs). Previous work has shown how to make this notion precise for representing binary concepts that have natural contrasts (e.g., {male, female}) as directions in representation space. However, many natural concepts do not have natural contrasts (e.g., whether the output is about an animal). In this work, we show how to extend the formalization of the linear representation hypothesis to represent features (e.g., is_animal) as vectors. This allows us to immediately formalize the representation of categorical concepts as polytopes in the representation space. Further, we use the formalization to prove a relationship between the hierarchical structure of concepts and the geometry of their representations. We validate these theoretical results on the Gemma and LLaMA-3 large language models, estimating representations for 900+ hierarchically related concepts using data from WordNet.

papers.title: Loop as a Bridge: Can Looped Transformers Truly Link Representation Space and Natural Language Outputs?
papers.research_question: Can Looped Transformers align linguistic verification output with representations? Can LTs enhance their introspective awareness on representations?
papers.core_contribution: Increasing loop iterations in Looped Transformers narrows the gap between self-verification and representation readout, but partly due to degradation of representation quality. Moreover, LTs only show introspective awareness in the final loop, not continuously across loops.
papers.conclusion: Current Looped Transformers do not yet achieve continuous introspection across loops, and the observed gap narrowing is partly driven by a degradation in representation quality.
papers.key_findings:
The accuracy of textual self-verification improves with more loop iterations.
The performance of representation-based linear probes declines with more loop iterations.
The gap between representation readout and self-verification narrows with more loops, but partly because of the decline in representation readout.
LTs are only aware of injected concepts when the injection occurs in the final loop, not in earlier loops.
papers.limitation: The experiments are a preliminary exploration conducted on a single specific implementation of LTs (Ouro), so the observed limitations should not be interpreted as intrinsic flaws of the general LTs paradigm.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often exhibit a gap between their internal knowledge and their explicit linguistic outputs. In this report, we empirically investigate whether Looped Transformers (LTs)--architectures that increase computational depth by iterating shared layers--can bridge this gap by utilizing their iterative nature as a form of introspection. Our experiments reveal that while increasing loop iterations narrows the gap, it is partly driven by a degradation of their internal knowledge carried by representations. Moreover, another empirical analysis suggests that current LTs' ability to perceive representations does not improve across loops; it is only present in the final loop. These results suggest that while LTs offer a promising direction for scaling computational depth, they have yet to achieve the introspection required to truly link representation space and natural language.

papers.title: Lost in Multilinguality: Dissecting Cross-lingual Factual Inconsistency in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the underlying causes of cross-lingual factual inconsistency in multilingual language models, and how can this inconsistency be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies that cross-lingual factual inconsistency in multilingual language models arises from failures in the language transition phase in the final layers, and proposes a linear shortcut method that bypasses these layers to improve both prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency.
papers.conclusion: Language transition errors are a key cause of cross-lingual inconsistency, and the proposed linear shortcut method effectively mitigates this issue, improving model consistency and accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual language models encode factual knowledge in a language-independent concept space through most layers, transitioning to language-specific spaces only in the final layers.
Incorrect predictions in the target language often occur due to failures during the language transition, even when the correct answer is present in the concept space.
The proposed linear shortcut method, which bypasses final-layer computations, enhances prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency.
The concept space in LLaMA2 is English-centric, while BLOOM's concept space is more linguistically diverse.
The knowledge recall process in multilingual models involves three stages: relation processing, object extraction in the latent language, and language-specific adaptation.
papers.limitation:
The analysis assumes English as the pivot language, which may limit applicability to language pairs that do not involve English.
The KLAR dataset covers 17 languages but does not fully capture the diversity of world languages.
The shortcut method relies on linear approximation; non-linear approaches might better capture complex transformations.
The study does not explore downstream applications such as multilingual knowledge localization or editing.
future_direction: Expand the investigation to more languages and additional language models to assess broader applicability.
Develop non-linear shortcut methods to better mitigate language transition errors.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models (MLMs) store factual knowledge across languages but often struggle to provide consistent responses to semantically equivalent prompts in different languages. While previous studies point out this cross-lingual inconsistency issue, the underlying causes remain unexplored. In this work, we use mechanistic interpretability methods to investigate cross-lingual inconsistencies in MLMs. We find that MLMs encode knowledge in a language-independent concept space through most layers, and only transition to language-specific spaces in the final layers. Failures during the language transition often result in incorrect predictions in the target language, even when the answers are correct in other languages. To mitigate this inconsistency issue, we propose a linear shortcut method that bypasses computations in the final layers, enhancing both prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency. Our findings shed light on the internal mechanisms of MLMs and provide a lightweight, effective strategy for producing more consistent factual outputs.

papers.title: Language Representation Projection: Can We Transfer Factual Knowledge across Languages in Multilingual Language Models?
papers.research_question: Can cross-lingual alignment of representation spaces enable factual knowledge transfer across languages? Specifically, can we transfer factual knowledge from English to non-English languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes LRP2, a parameter-free method that projects representations between languages to align representation spaces, which improves factual knowledge retrieval and transfer across languages in multilingual language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper confirms that cross-lingual alignment of representation spaces enables factual knowledge transfer across languages, and proposes LRP2 as an effective method for this transfer.
papers.key_findings:
LRP2 improves factual knowledge retrieval accuracy and cross-lingual transferability for non-English languages.
LRP2 aligns representation spaces: LIRP projects non-English representations to English-like ones, and LSRP projects them back to the non-English space.
LRP2 increases the overlap of knowledge neurons between English and non-English languages, indicating enhanced cross-lingual knowledge transfer.
Cross-lingual knowledge neurons exist in multilingual pretrained language models.
Different languages require different optimal layer configurations for the LIRP and LSRP modules, indicating varying degrees of representation alignment needed.
papers.limitation:
The effectiveness of LRP2 heavily relies on the inherent capabilities of multilingual pretrained language models.
Experiments are limited to two relatively small models due to limited compute resources.
future_direction: Investigate LRP2 on larger language models.
papers.abstract: Multilingual pretrained language models serve as repositories of multilingual factual knowledge. Nevertheless, a substantial performance gap of factual knowledge probing exists between high-resource languages and low-resource languages, suggesting limited implicit factual knowledge transfer across languages in multilingual pretrained language models. This paper investigates the feasibility of explicitly transferring relatively rich factual knowledge from English to non-English languages. To accomplish this, we propose two parameter-free Language Representation Projection modules (LRP2). The first module converts non-English representations into English-like equivalents, while the second module reverts English-like representations back into representations of the corresponding non-English language. Experimental results on the mLAMA dataset demonstrate that LRP2 significantly improves factual knowledge retrieval accuracy and facilitates knowledge transferability across diverse non-English languages. We further investigate the working mechanism of LRP2 from the perspectives of representation space and cross-lingual knowledge neuron.

papers.title: Exploring Concept Depth: How Large Language Models Acquire Knowledge and Concept at Different Layers?
papers.research_question: Can shallow layers in LLMs capture meaningful features of simple knowledge, while complex concepts need deeper layers to capture their meaningful features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of 'Concept Depth' to measure how different layers in LLMs capture concepts of varying complexity, showing that simpler concepts are learned in shallow layers while complex concepts require deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: The Concept Depth metric provides a useful framework for understanding how LLMs process concepts of varying complexity across layers, and the experimental insights enhance the understanding of internal representations in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler concepts (e.g., factual knowledge) are learned in shallow layers, while more complex concepts (e.g., reasoning tasks) require deeper layers for accurate understanding.
The pattern of Concept Depth is consistent across different model families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) and model sizes.
Larger models within a family tend to achieve higher peak accuracy and sometimes converge to optimal performance at earlier layers.
Adding noise to the input or quantizing model weights (e.g., to 8-bit) slows down the convergence of concept understanding, requiring deeper layers to achieve comparable accuracy.
Compressing models to 16-bit quantization does not significantly harm the understanding process compared to 32-bit.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performances across a wide range of tasks. However, the mechanisms by which these models encode tasks of varying complexities remain poorly understood. In this paper, we explore the hypothesis that LLMs process concepts of varying complexities in different layers, introducing the idea of "Concept Depth" to suggest that more complex concepts are typically acquired in deeper layers. Specifically, we categorize concepts based on their level of abstraction, defining them in the order of increasing complexity within factual, emotional, and inferential tasks. We conduct extensive probing experiments using layer-wise representations across various LLM families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) on various datasets spanning the three domains of tasks. Our findings reveal that models could efficiently conduct probing for simpler tasks in shallow layers, and more complex tasks typically necessitate deeper layers for accurate understanding. Additionally, we examine how external factors, such as adding noise to the input and quantizing the model weights, might affect layer-wise representations. Our findings suggest that these factors can impede the development of a conceptual understanding of LLMs until deeper layers are explored. We hope that our proposed concept and experimental insights will enhance the understanding of the mechanisms underlying LLMs. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Luckfort/CD.

papers.title: Same Neurons, Different Languages: Probing Morphosyntax in Multilingual Pre-trained Models
papers.research_question: Does multilingual pre-trained models encode morphosyntactic information in the same subset of neurons across different languages?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual pre-trained models develop cross-lingually entangled representations of morphosyntax, with neuron overlap varying by category and influenced by language proximity and pre-training data size.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual pre-trained models implicitly align morphosyntactic information across languages by using overlapping subsets of neurons, which may affect their cross-lingual transfer capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Significant cross-lingual overlap exists in neurons encoding morphosyntactic information.
Overlap varies across morphosyntactic categories and is lower for categories with larger inventories of possible values.
Overlap is higher for languages within the same genus or with similar typological features.
Overlap increases with pre-training data size but decreases with larger model size (comparing XLM-R-base and XLM-R-large).
XLM-R-base tends to share more neurons than m-BERT for encoding morphosyntactic attributes.
future_direction: Artificially encouraging neuron overlap to facilitate zero-shot cross-lingual inference to low-resource and typologically distant languages.
papers.abstract: The success of multilingual pre-trained models is underpinned by their ability to learn representations shared by multiple languages even in absence of any explicit supervision. However, it remains unclear how these models learn to generalise across languages. In this work, we conjecture that multilingual pre-trained models can derive language-universal abstractions about grammar. In particular, we investigate whether morphosyntactic information is encoded in the same subset of neurons in different languages. We conduct the first large-scale empirical study over 43 languages and 14 morphosyntactic categories with a state-of-the-art neuron-level probe. Our findings show that the cross-lingual overlap between neurons is significant, but its extent may vary across categories and depends on language proximity and pre-training data size.

papers.title: Models of Visually Grounded Speech Signal Pay Attention to Nouns: A Bilingual Experiment on English and Japanese
papers.research_question: What is the behavior of attention in neural models of visually grounded speech trained on English and Japanese, and does it focus on nouns?
papers.core_contribution: Shows that attention in neural models of visually grounded speech focuses on nouns across English and Japanese, and demonstrates cross-lingual speech retrieval using images as pivots.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that attention in visually grounded speech models focuses on nouns across languages, with language-specific adaptations, and enables cross-lingual retrieval using images as pivots.
papers.key_findings:
Attention primarily focuses on nouns in both English and Japanese models.
The Japanese model also pays attention to particles, developing a language-specific behavior similar to human toddlers.
Attention peaks are located at word endings in English and at both beginnings and endings in Japanese.
Images can be used as pivots for cross-lingual speech-to-speech retrieval without parallel data.
The model exhibits noun-bias, aligning with theories of child language acquisition.
papers.limitation: The study uses synthetic speech with only one voice, whereas prior work used real speech with multiple speakers.
future_direction: Validate the methodology on a bilingual dataset featuring real voices.
Extract a bilingual speech-to-speech dictionary using attention peaks as anchor points.
papers.abstract: We investigate the behaviour of attention in neural models of visually grounded speech trained on two languages: English and Japanese. Experimental results show that attention focuses on nouns and this behaviour holds true for two very typologically different languages. We also draw parallels between artificial neural attention and human attention and show that neural attention focuses on word endings as it has been theorised for human attention. Finally, we investigate how two visually grounded monolingual models can be used to perform cross-lingual speech-to-speech retrieval. For both languages, the enriched bilingual (speech-image) corpora with part-of-speech tags and forced alignments are distributed to the community for reproducible research.

papers.title: Tracing the complexity profiles of different linguistic phenomena through the intrinsic dimension of LLM representations
papers.research_question: Does the intrinsic dimension (ID) of LLM representations serve as a marker for linguistic complexity, and can it differentiate between formal and functional complexity?
papers.core_contribution: The intrinsic dimension (ID) of LLM representations is a useful marker for linguistic complexity, allowing differentiation between formal and functional complexity, and points to similar stages of linguistic processing across disparate LLMs.
papers.conclusion: ID is a useful marker of linguistic complexity in LLMs, it allows differentiation between formal and functional complexity, and it points to similar stages of linguistic processing across disparate LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
ID profiles differentiate between formal complexity (coordination vs. subordination) and functional complexity (right-branching vs. center-embedding, unambiguous vs. ambiguous).
The formal complexity contrast emerges in layers coinciding with the generic ID peak, a phase of deep linguistic processing.
Functional complexity contrasts are also reflected in ID but in a less marked way and not correlated with the same processing phase.
Representational similarity (Information Imbalance) and ablation experiments confirm these trends.
Different LLMs show consistent ID profiles and processing stages.
papers.limitation:
Due to compute restrictions, experiments cannot be extended to larger language models.
Results should be reproduced in languages other than English and with more naturalistic data.
A clear mechanistic explanation of the relation between intrinsic dimension and the linguistic phenomena is needed.
future_direction: Ascertain the extent to which observed patterns depend on model size and their emergence during training.
Reproduce results in languages other than English and with more naturalistic data.
Establish a clear mechanistic explanation of the relation between intrinsic dimension and linguistic phenomena.
papers.abstract: We explore the intrinsic dimension (ID) of LLM representations as a marker of linguistic complexity, asking if different ID profiles across LLM layers differentially characterize formal and functional complexity. We find the formal contrast between sentences with multiple coordinated or subordinated clauses to be reflected in ID differences whose onset aligns with a phase of more abstract linguistic processing independently identified in earlier work. The functional contrasts between sentences characterized by right branching vs. center embedding or unambiguous vs. ambiguous relative clause attachment are also picked up by ID, but in a less marked way, and they do not correlate with the same processing phase. Further experiments using representational similarity and layer ablation confirm the same trends. We conclude that ID is a useful marker of linguistic complexity in LLMs, that it allows to differentiate between different types of complexity, and that it points to similar stages of linguistic processing across disparate LLMs.

papers.title: Echoes of BERT: Do Modern Language Models Rediscover the Classical NLP Pipeline?
papers.research_question: How do modern language models encode linguistic structure, and do they rediscover the classical NLP pipeline observed in earlier models like BERT?
papers.core_contribution: Modern language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline, with lexical information concentrated in early layers and becoming nonlinear, while inflectional morphology remains linearly accessible across layers and languages.
papers.conclusion: Modern transformer language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline and exhibit robust representational regularities for lexical and inflectional information across architectures, sizes, and languages.
papers.key_findings:
Modern LMs consistently organize linguistic information hierarchically: early layers process syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entities, later layers capture discourse.
Lexical identity (lemma) information is most accessible in early layers and becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network.
Inflectional morphology remains highly linearly accessible across all layers and across six typologically diverse languages.
These representational patterns emerge early during pretraining and are robust across model architectures, sizes, and training regimes.
Inflectional features occupy compact, linearly accessible subspaces in the residual stream, enabling effective steering interventions.
papers.limitation:
Representation extraction for decoder-only models uses the final subword token, which may not be optimal for all architectures.
The study does not explicitly examine cases where different grammatical functions share the same surface form (e.g., infinitive and non-past verb forms).
Classifiers only detect correlations in hidden activations, not causal mechanisms.
Steering experiments measure changes in classifier performance rather than downstream model outputs.
future_direction: Develop better extraction methods for word representations from decoder-only models.
Examine how models separate form from function across languages in cases of surface-form ambiguity.
Design more complex experiments to evaluate steering effects on actual model generation.
papers.abstract: Large transformer-based language models dominate modern NLP, yet our understanding of how they encode linguistic information relies primarily on studies of early models like BERT and GPT-2. Building on classic BERTology work, we analyze 25 models spanning from classical architectures (BERT, DeBERTa, GPT-2) to modern large language models (Pythia, OLMo-2, Gemma-2, Qwen2.5, Llama-3.1), probing layer-by-layer representations across eight linguistic tasks in English. Consistent with earlier findings, we find that hierarchical organization persists in modern models: early layers capture syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entity-level information, and later layers encode discourse phenomena. We dive deeper, conducting an in-depth multilingual analysis of two specific linguistic properties - lexical identity and inflectional morphology - that help disentangle form from meaning. We find that lexical information concentrates linearly in early layers but becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network, while inflectional information remains linearly accessible throughout all layers. Additional analyses of attention mechanisms, steering vectors, and pretraining checkpoints reveal where this information resides within layers, how it can be functionally manipulated, and how representations evolve during pretraining. Taken together, our findings suggest that, even with substantial advances in LLM technologies, transformer models learn to organize linguistic information in similar ways, regardless of model architecture, size, or training regime, indicating that these properties are important for next token prediction. Our code is available at https://github.com/ml5885/model_internal_sleuthing

papers.title: Deconstructing multimodality: visual properties and visual context in human semantic processing
papers.research_question: Whether differentiating between internal visual properties and external visual context is beneficial compared to learning visual representations from complete images for decoding brain activity associated with noun meanings.
papers.core_contribution: Multimodal semantic models that differentiate between internal and external visual features correlate with human neural semantic representations, and internal visual features are most important for decoding brain activity associated with concrete nouns.
papers.conclusion: Internal visual features are superior for decoding brain activity associated with concrete nouns, and automatic object detection techniques can produce high-quality visual representations, reducing reliance on manually annotated datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Models using internal visual features (VIS-INTERNAL) outperform those using external or whole-image features in decoding brain activity.
Multimodal models combining linguistic and visual information (MM-INTERNAL, MM-EXTERNAL) perform better than visual-only models.
The combined multimodal model (MM-COMBINED) outperforms the whole-image multimodal model.
Models using automatically annotated images perform on par with those using manually annotated images, demonstrating the utility of automatic object detection.
papers.abstract: Multimodal semantic models that extend linguistic representations with additional perceptual input have proved successful in a range of natural language processing (NLP) tasks. Recent research has successfully used neural methods to automatically create visual representations for words. However, these works have extracted visual features from complete images, and have not examined how different kinds of visual information impact performance. In contrast, we construct multimodal models that differentiate between internal visual properties of the objects and their external visual context. We evaluate the models on the task of decoding brain activity associated with the meanings of nouns, demonstrating their advantage over those based on complete images.
